open-question.question: Does an install or update of the Gurita plugin started from the Settings window run in a terminal the person can watch, as a recipe run does, or as a background process like the harness check, with the window reporting how it ended?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: No install or update command has been run against a harness yet, so the form that shows every line and lets a prompt be answered holds whatever the commands turn out to print or ask; it reuses the terminal a recipe run starts in, and the exit status VS Code gives for a closed terminal lets the window report the end.
open-question.alternative: An install or update runs in a terminal the extension opens and shows, as in a recipe run, its output and any prompt visible and answerable there, and the extension also watches that terminal's process end (its exit status, through the terminal or a VS Code task run in the terminal panel) and the window then reports how it ended, success or failure, beside the harness or in a notification. It gives the person both the full live output, with prompts answerable, and an outcome the window states without anyone reading the terminal, so an unexpected prompt or long download stays visible while the window still knows whether the install succeeded. The run terminals today report only that they closed, never an exit status, so the extension gains a second terminal mechanism with exit-status tracking; the window can tell success from failure only by the exit code, so a command that exits 0 after printing a warning reads as a success, and the reported reason for a failure is whatever the person reads in the terminal.

An install or update runs in a terminal the extension opens and shows, as a recipe run does: the terminal's own process runs the harness's install or update commands in the runner's session shell at the project root, its output and any prompt visible and answerable there. The window learns only that the terminal was started and, at most, that it closed; it reports no outcome of its own, and the person reads how it ended in the terminal. It reuses the one way the extension already starts long, visible work (`src/runs.ts` launching a terminal), so every line the CLIs print and any prompt they raise reach the person directly, which matters while no install or update command has yet been run against a harness and what each prints or asks is unobserved. The window has no outcome to show beside the harness, so a failed install looks the same in the Settings window as a successful one until the person reads the terminal or uses Check again; and it leaves a terminal per install for the person to read and close.

An install or update runs as a child process with no terminal, as the harness check does: started through `execFile` into the runner's session shell (`$SHELL -i` for the sh, bash, zsh family) at the project root with a time limit, its input closed and the commands given their non-interactive flags (such as `-y`), its output captured and not shown. While it runs the window shows the harness as busy and disables its controls, and when it ends the window reports success or failure, the failure with the captured error text, in the harness's line or an error notification as other edits' failures are told. It keeps the whole action inside the Settings window, mirrors the harness check's tested pattern (session shell, captured print, a stated result), and gives the window the exit status and the error text to report, with no terminal for the person to manage. Nothing the commands print is visible while they run, so a slow download looks stalled and a command that waits on a prompt hangs until the time limit; whether the CLIs prompt or run long is unobserved, the condition the hands-on command verification question settles.

An install or update runs as a background child process in the runner's session shell, as the harness check does, its input closed and the commands given their non-interactive flags, but its output is streamed line by line into a VS Code output channel of the extension's, which the person can open while it runs and which is brought forward when the run fails. The window shows the harness as busy while it runs and, when it ends, reports success or failure beside the harness or in a notification. The window owns the outcome as in a plain background run, while every line the commands print stays available on demand and surfaces by itself on a failure, so a stall or an unexpected message can be diagnosed without a terminal per install. It adds an output channel, a mechanism the extension does not use today, and streaming instead of the check's captured print; like any background run it cannot answer a prompt, so a command that asks for input hangs until the time limit, the condition the hands-on command verification question settles.

open-question.question: For a harness that has a Gurita copy installed, is the Update control in the Settings window offered always, or only when the installed copy's version is found to differ from the version it is compared with?
open-question.recommendation: Update fetches the latest published release whatever the installed copy is compared with, so gating it on that comparison would hide it where a newer release exists or a version could not be read; an update over a current copy costs one harmless run and repairs a damaged copy.
open-question.alternative: Update is offered for every harness whose check found the CLI and an installed Gurita copy. The version comparison does not gate it: a copy whose version matches the compared version gets the same enabled Update control as one that differs, and the check line beside it still reports whether the versions differ. Whatever the comparison baseline turns out to be, the person can always bring a copy to the latest published release. A matching packaged version does not mean the copy is the latest published one, a version that could not be read does not hide the control, and running Update over a matching copy re-fetches the release, which also repairs a damaged copy (on Antigravity, re-extracting the archive). The window also needs no version rule of its own and no state for the control to go stale against. The control does not tell the person whether updating will change anything, so they may run an install that is a no-op (Claude Code's `claude plugin update` on a current copy, for example) or start one they did not need. Whether that clutter or wasted run matters depends on how an update runs and whether it asks for confirmation, both axes sibling questions own.

Update is offered only when the installed copy's version differs from the version it is compared with, in either direction. It is not offered when the two are equal. When the comparison cannot be made, because the installed version or the compared version could not be read, Update is offered. The control appears exactly when the check already reports a version difference, so the two agree and an equal copy gets no pointless update. Failing open means an unreadable version or a failed read of the compared version never leaves the person with no way to update. A copy whose version equals the compared version can never be updated or repaired from the window. If the comparison is with the packaged version, a copy equal to the packaged version gets no Update even when a newer release has been published. That depends on the comparison baseline, an axis a sibling question owns. Treating any difference as a reason to update also offers an update to a copy newer than the compared version, which could move it to an older release when the compared version is the latest published one.

Update is offered only when the installed copy's version differs from the version it is compared with, in either direction. It is not offered when the two are equal, and it is not offered when the comparison cannot be made because either version could not be read. Update is offered only when the window has positive evidence that the copy is out of line, so a click on it always has a known version difference behind it and the control never invites an update the window cannot justify. A failed or not-yet-made read blocks updates: a listing error, a version the check could not read, or a compared version read only when asked for or not reachable over the network leaves no update path in the window. How often that happens depends on the comparison baseline and when it is read, axes a sibling question owns. The equal-version and newer-copy costs of the previous option apply here too.

Update is offered only when the installed copy's version is older than the version it is compared with, read as a MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH ordering. It is not offered when the copy is equal or newer. When the comparison cannot be made, because a version could not be read or does not parse as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, Update is offered. The window never invites an update that would move a copy backwards, for example a copy ahead of the published release or newer than the packaged version, while an unreadable version still leaves an update path. The window needs a version ordering of its own, beyond the equality the check compares today, and a copy that is equal or newer can never be updated or repaired from the window. As with any gated option, a copy equal to the packaged version gets no Update when a newer release exists if the comparison is with the packaged version. That depends on the comparison baseline, an axis a sibling question owns.

Update is offered only when the installed copy's version is older than the version it is compared with, read as a MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH ordering. It is not offered when the copy is equal or newer, and it is not offered when the comparison cannot be made because a version could not be read or does not parse. This is the strictest gate: Update appears only when the window knows the copy is behind, so every update it offers moves the copy forward and none is speculative. It combines the costs of the other gates: the window needs a version ordering of its own, equal and newer copies can never be updated or repaired, and any failed or not-yet-made version read leaves no update path. How often that read is missing depends on the comparison baseline and when it is read, axes a sibling question owns.

open-question.question: A harness's existing Gurita copy, or its marketplace named `gurita`, may come from somewhere other than the distribution repository, for example a local checkout registered as a directory marketplace under the same name and plugin id. What does Install or Update in the Settings window do on such a harness: switch it to the distribution repository, update from the source already registered, or refuse and say why?
open-question.recommendation: The window promises the published release from the distribution repository, and on a harness registered to another source it could keep that promise only by replacing a registration someone made on purpose; refusing, naming the source found, and giving the commands that switch by hand breaks no development setup and never reports a published install that was not made.
open-question.alternative: The window detects a foreign source as in Switch to distribution and, for that harness, neither installs nor updates: the control is refused (or not offered) and the window states the source found and the CLI commands that would switch the harness to its distribution repository. Harnesses registered to the distribution repository, or holding no `gurita` marketplace, are installed and updated as usual. On Antigravity, whose listing names no source, the copy is acted on like any other. No development setup is ever replaced and the window never claims to have installed the published release when it did not, while the person learns exactly why and how to switch by hand. On the machine that builds the extension, where every copy comes from the checkout, the new controls do nothing, and the harness check has to read the marketplace registrations it does not read today, adding a listing call per harness to the 120-second check session.

The window detects a foreign source (on Claude Code a `gurita` marketplace that `claude plugin marketplace list --json` gives as other than `uHappyLogic/gurita-claude`, or a copy carrying `readFromFolder`; on Codex a `gurita` marketplace rooted at a local path or another repository) and on both Install and Update re-registers the `gurita` marketplace to the harness's distribution repository, replacing the existing registration, then installs or updates from it. The person is told afterwards that the source was switched. On Antigravity, whose listing names no source, the copy at `~/.gemini/config/plugins/gurita` is acted on like any other. Every Install and Update ends with the latest published release from the distribution repository, exactly as the goal states, whatever the harness held before, so the window's outcome is one thing on every machine. It silently dismantles a development setup such as this machine's, where all three copies are read from the checkout; replacing a Claude Code marketplace may drop or orphan copies installed from it at other scopes and projects, and at project scope it changes the tracked `.claude/settings.json`; what each CLI does when an already-registered name is re-added or removed is unobserved.

The window detects nothing and changes no registration: Install installs `gurita@gurita` from the `gurita` marketplace already registered when one exists, adding the distribution repository only when none is, and Update refreshes the registered marketplace (`claude plugin marketplace update gurita`, `codex plugin marketplace upgrade gurita`) and updates the copy from it, whatever that source is. On Antigravity, whose listing names no source, the copy is acted on like any other. It never overwrites a registration the person made on purpose, so a maintainer working from a local checkout keeps the setup the copy is read from, and it needs no source detection in the check. On a harness registered to a checkout, Install and Update bring in whatever the checkout holds rather than the latest published release, contrary to the goal, and a directory source may change nothing at all while the window reports success; the version the copy then shows may still differ from the one it is compared with.

The window detects a foreign source as in Switch to distribution and, at the click on Install or Update for that harness, asks in a VS Code prompt whether to switch the `gurita` marketplace to the distribution repository, to update from the source already registered, or to cancel, then does what was chosen; harnesses already on the distribution repository get no such prompt. On Antigravity, whose listing names no source, the copy is acted on like any other. Both legitimate wishes are served from the window, a user moving to the published release and a maintainer refreshing from the checkout, and neither a silent replacement nor a dead end occurs. It carries the detection cost and both the switching and the registered-source code paths, each with its own unobserved CLI behaviour to build against and test, plus a prompt whose interplay with any confirmation the window asks before an install has to be settled beside it (an axis the confirmation question owns).

The window detects a foreign source as in Switch to distribution and splits by action: Install, offered where no copy stands, re-registers the `gurita` marketplace to the distribution repository before installing, while Update leaves the registration as it is and updates the existing copy from the source already registered. On Antigravity, whose listing names no source, the copy is acted on like any other. A copy someone installed from a checkout is never replaced behind their back, yet a fresh Install always yields the published release even on a harness whose marketplace name was taken by an earlier local registration. Update on a checkout-sourced copy still does not bring the published release, and on Claude Code re-registering the user-scope marketplace for an Install changes the source of copies already installed from it at other scopes or projects; whether that case arises depends on whether Install is offered beside an existing copy (an axis the install-beside-existing-copy question owns).

The window gives the case no behaviour of its own: it neither detects the source nor refuses, and runs the same install or update commands it runs everywhere, against the distribution repository, leaving whatever each CLI does with an already-registered `gurita` marketplace or a folder-read copy to decide the outcome, which the window reports as the command ended. It is the least code and the least to test, and it adds no read to the harness check, the case being rare outside the maintainer's own machine. The outcome is whatever each CLI happens to do, unobserved today and possibly different per harness: a re-add may fail on the taken name, replace the registration silently, or update from the checkout while the window says the latest release was installed, so the person cannot predict or understand what happened.

open-question.question: How does the person pick the scope of a Claude Code install (user, project, or local) in the Settings window, whose page holds buttons and dropdowns only?
open-question.recommendation: The scope is chosen at the moment of installing, in VS Code's own picker as every typed value goes through its input box, with room to say where each scope is recorded, so a project-scope write to the tracked settings file is never made unread; the page keeps one Install control per harness.
open-question.alternative: The Claude Code row carries one Install control like the other harnesses; clicking it opens VS Code's own quick pick (`showQuickPick`, which the extension already uses to pick a starting variant) listing user, project, and local, each with a one-line description of where it is recorded (user settings, the project's shared `.claude/settings.json`, the project's local settings), and the install runs at the scope picked, a dismissed pick installing nothing; nothing is selected or stored on the page. The page keeps one Install control per harness and the choice is made at the moment of installing with room to explain each scope, so a project-scope write to a tracked file is never made without the person reading what it means. Every Claude Code install costs a second step and moves the choice out of the page into a picker the page tests cannot draw, so the stubbed `showQuickPick` becomes the only test of it; whether the picker also serves as the confirmation before installing depends on the sibling question on confirmation before install.

The Claude Code row of the Harnesses part carries a scope dropdown (a `select` of user, project, and local) beside its Install control, the form the page already uses for its model, effort, and harness dropdowns; the selection lives in the page's state for the window's session only, is stored nowhere, starts at user (the CLI's own default for `claude plugin install -s`), and a click on Install installs at the scope the dropdown shows. The scope is visible before the click and uses a control the page already draws and tests, so the person sees exactly what Install will do with no extra dialog step and nothing new is persisted. The row gains a control that only Claude Code has, and a person who clicks Install without looking installs at user scope by default; which scopes the dropdown lists while a copy already stands, or while no folder is open, depends on the sibling questions on installing beside an existing copy and on project scopes without a project.

The Claude Code row carries a scope dropdown (user, project, local) whose value is a stored setting in the per-user `~/.gurita/variants.json`, where everything else the settings hold is kept, read back on every opening of the window and used by every Install until the person changes it; the first value is user. A person who always installs at one scope sets it once and every later install from any window or session follows it, consistent with the rule that the settings' values are kept in `variants.json`. A per-user stored value is applied to every project, so a project or local choice made for one repository silently carries into the next, where it writes that project's `.claude/settings.json` or local settings unasked; it adds a stored field and its read and write path to the settings file for a choice that is usually made once per install, and whether Update also follows it depends on the sibling question on update target scopes.

The Claude Code row carries no dropdown and instead three install controls, Install at user, Install at project, and Install at local, each installing at its own scope on a click, with nothing selected or stored. The scope is part of the control the person clicks, so there is no default to fall into and no hidden state, and each control can be enabled or disabled on its own as the scope's situation requires. Three buttons crowd one row where the other harnesses show a single Install, and the row grows further if update controls follow the same per-scope pattern; which of the three are shown or enabled depends on the sibling questions on installing beside an existing copy and on project scopes without a project.

open-question.question: When Claude Code already holds a Gurita copy at one scope, does the Settings window still offer installing at the other scopes, or is Install offered only while no copy applies to the open project?
open-question.recommendation: The goal offers all three of Claude Code's scopes and expects copies at several, so the window withholds none that stands free; a project copy pinned for a team beside a personal user copy is the arrangement this repository itself holds, and the per-scope detection it needs is the one showing the detected scopes needs anyway.
open-question.alternative: While Claude Code holds a Gurita copy at one or more scopes that apply to the open project, the Settings window still offers Install for Claude Code, at every one of the three scopes (user, project, local) that holds no copy applying to the project, whether that scope is more or less specific than the copy that wins; a scope already holding an applying copy is not offered for Install, that copy being reached through Update. Copies at project or local scope recorded for other project roots do not count, since they do not apply to the open project. It offers exactly the scopes Claude Code itself supports and leaves the person free to add any of them, such as a project-scope copy pinned in the tracked `.claude/settings.json` for teammates beside a personal user-scope copy (the arrangement this machine already holds), so the window never withholds a native install path. It lets the window create several copies at once, so a person can install a more specific copy that silently shadows the one in use, or a less specific one that changes nothing for the open project, and every multi-copy question (which copy Update acts on, how several scopes are shown) becomes reachable from the window itself; the window also needs per-scope detection, which today's check, reporting one copy and no scope, does not give.

While a copy applies to the open project, Install is offered only at the scopes more specific than the copy that wins for the project, in Claude Code's own order (local over project over user): with a user-scope winner, project and local are offered; with a project-scope winner, local alone; with a local-scope winner, no Install is offered. Less specific scopes are not offered while a copy applies. Every install the window offers is one that takes effect in the open project, replacing the copy that wins there, so no click produces a copy the person cannot see working from where they clicked it. A person holding only a project or local copy cannot add a user-scope copy for all their projects from this project's window and must open a project with no applying copy or use the CLI, and each offered install shadows the existing copy, which may then sit unused at its own version; it too needs the winning copy's scope, which today's check does not report.

While a copy applies to the open project, Install is offered only at the scopes less specific than the copy that wins for the project: with a local-scope winner, project and user are offered; with a project-scope winner, user alone; with a user-scope winner, no Install is offered. More specific scopes are not offered while a copy applies. No install from the window changes which copy the open project runs, so adding a copy beside an existing one can never displace the copy the person's runs already use; it still covers the common case of widening a project-only copy to the user scope. The copy it installs never shows its effect in the open project, so the window would report an install the person cannot observe from here, and pinning a project or local copy over an existing user copy (a team's tracked `.claude/settings.json` entry) is never offered beside a user-scope copy.

alternative.id: No Install once a copy applies

open-question.alternative: Install for Claude Code is offered only while no Gurita copy applies to the open project; as soon as one does, at any scope, Install is not offered at any scope and the existing copy is reached only through Update. Adding a copy at another scope beside it is left to the CLI. It is the simplest model: one control per state (Install when absent, Update when present), the window never creates a second copy, and it needs only the check's existing installed-or-not answer to decide, not per-scope detection. It withholds scopes the goal says Claude Code offers natively, so a person with a user-scope copy who wants a project-scope copy for the repository must leave the window for the CLI; how a copy counts as applying when the winning entry is disabled is a condition owned by the disabled-copy question.

open-question.question: When Claude Code holds Gurita copies at more than one scope that applies to the open project, which does Update in the Settings window act on: every detected scope, only the copy that wins for the project, or one scope the person picks?
open-question.recommendation: Update means bringing Gurita on the harness to the latest release, and a copy left at an old version goes on serving other projects and returns as this project's copy once the winning entry is removed; one click that updates every applying copy leaves none stale and asks the person nothing.
open-question.alternative: One click on Update acts on every scope at which a Gurita copy was detected for the open project: the user entry and each project or local entry whose projectPath equals the project root. The window runs one scoped update per such scope (claude plugin update gurita@gurita -s user, then -s project, then -s local, as detected) in one run, and the person chooses nothing about scope. No copy that applies to the project is left at the old release. The check's winning copy and every less specific copy end on the same version, so a later winner change, such as a local entry removed, never brings back a stale copy. On this machine, which holds user and project entries, one click covers both. It changes scopes the person may not have meant to touch. Updating the user scope changes the copy every other project on the machine uses, and the project scope belongs to the repository's shared setup. One run issues several CLI calls, so the window must say how a run ends when one scope's update fails and another succeeds. Which scopes count as detected depends on the Disabled Claude Code copy question: is a scope holding only a disabled copy updated too?

Update acts only on the one copy the harness check already picks for the project root, local over project over user. The window runs claude plugin update gurita@gurita -s with that copy's scope, and leaves every less specific copy as it stands. The person chooses nothing about scope. It updates exactly the copy this project's harness sessions load, which is also the copy whose version the check reports. It touches nothing else, so the user scope other projects use and any second project-level entry stay as they were, and the run is one CLI call with one outcome. Less specific copies stay at the old release. A user-scope copy left stale goes on serving every other project, and it becomes this project's copy again once the winning entry is removed. The person may also not see that anything was left behind, depending on what the Several-scope display question shows next to each scope. And when the winner is disabled, which scope is "the winner" turns on the Disabled Claude Code copy question.

Update acts on one scope per click, and the person chooses it from the detected scopes only, either from a dropdown beside Update or through one Update control per detected scope. Each click runs one claude plugin update gurita@gurita -s with the chosen scope. No single action updates several scopes, and updating every scope takes one click per scope. The person sees and chooses each scope that changes, so the user scope other projects share and the repository's project scope are never changed as a side effect. Each run is still one CLI call with one outcome. It adds a scope control to Update and puts a choice on the person in the most common case too: a person who just wants everything current has to click once per scope. The choice is only informed if the window shows which scope is stale, which depends on the Several-scope display question (scope names alone, or each scope with its own version) and on the Update control availability question.

The person chooses Update's target from a dropdown that lists each detected scope alone plus one choice covering every detected scope. A single-scope choice runs one claude plugin update gurita@gurita -s with that scope. The all-scopes choice runs one scoped update per detected scope in one run. Both needs are met by one control. A person who wants everything current gets it in one click, and a person who wants to leave the user scope or the shared project scope alone can still update only the copy they mean. It is the largest control of the set: one more dropdown with one more choice to draw, test, and document. Its all-scopes choice also carries the same partial-failure reporting as Every detected scope. Whether a single-scope choice is an informed one again depends on the Several-scope display question.

The window passes no scope at all. Update runs claude plugin update gurita@gurita without -s, so Claude Code's own default (auto-detect) decides which copy or copies it updates, and the window neither chooses the scope nor lets the person choose it. The extension holds no scope rule of its own for Update and follows the harness's own update path exactly, so if Claude Code changes how it resolves a scope, the window follows without any change. What auto-detect acts on when several scopes hold a copy has not been observed. It may be neither the winner the check reports nor every scope, and the window cannot say beforehand which copy will change. So whether this option is viable depends on what the Hands-on command verification question observes.

When more than one applicable scope holds a Gurita copy, the window offers no Update for Claude Code. It says that copies stand at several scopes and names the claude plugin update command with its -s option for the person to run. Update is offered only while exactly one applicable scope holds a copy, and then acts on that scope. This is meant as a permanent rule, not a postponement. The window never has to resolve the ambiguity, so it can never change a scope the person did not mean. Its Update code handles one scope and one outcome only. The case it gives up is a real one: this machine holds user and project copies for this repository today, so the maintainer's own setup could not update from the window. The person also has to leave the window for the terminal exactly when updating is most involved, which cuts against the goal of installing and updating from Settings.

open-question.question: For a Claude Code install at project or local scope made from the Settings window, at which scope is the `gurita` marketplace registered: the user scope, where `claude plugin install --marketplace` adds a marketplace not yet known, or the same scope as the install, through `claude plugin marketplace add --scope`?
open-question.alternative: The `gurita` marketplace is registered at user scope whatever scope the install is made at: a project or local install runs `claude plugin install gurita --marketplace uHappyLogic/gurita-claude --scope <project|local>`, which adds a marketplace not yet known in user settings before installing, and a marketplace already known at user scope is reused as it stands. No `claude plugin marketplace add` is run, and nothing about the marketplace is written to the project's `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json`; only the plugin's own entry lands at the install scope. One command per install, exactly the CLI's own documented behaviour for `--marketplace`, and the marketplace is declared once for every project on the machine, so a later install at any scope or project, and `claude plugin marketplace update gurita`, find it without a second registration. A project-scope install writes `"gurita@gurita": true` into the shared, committed `.claude/settings.json` with no declaration of where `gurita` comes from, so a teammate cloning the project has an enabled plugin whose marketplace their own Claude Code does not know; and a person who chose a project or local install also gets a user-level registration they did not ask for, which a later person-wide install or listing then sees.

The `gurita` marketplace is registered at the same scope as the install: the window first runs `claude plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/gurita-claude --scope <project|local>`, declaring it in `.claude/settings.json` for a project install or `.claude/settings.local.json` for a local one, then `claude plugin install gurita@gurita --scope <project|local>`, whether or not the marketplace is already known at user scope. A user-scope install registers at user scope as today. Each scope's settings file is self-contained: a project install's committed `.claude/settings.json` carries both the plugin entry and its marketplace source, so a teammate who clones the project is offered the same distribution repository, and a local install leaves no trace outside that project's private file. Two commands per install where one would do, a second write into the shared, committed `.claude/settings.json` beyond the plugin entry, and one marketplace name possibly declared at several scopes at once, whose interplay (which declaration `marketplace update` refreshes, whether a same-named declaration at another scope is refused) is unobserved; how the mission observes that before building on it is the hands-on verification question's axis.

alternative.id: Project at project, local at user

open-question.alternative: The scope of the registration follows whether the install is shared: a project-scope install declares the marketplace at project scope through `claude plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/gurita-claude --scope project` before `claude plugin install gurita@gurita --scope project`, while a local-scope install runs `claude plugin install gurita --marketplace uHappyLogic/gurita-claude --scope local`, registering at user scope when not yet known and reusing a user-scope registration otherwise. Nothing about the marketplace is written to `.claude/settings.local.json`. The committed file that teammates share carries the marketplace source it needs, while the private local install, whose only user is the person on this machine, takes the single-command path and leaves one reusable user-level registration rather than a per-project private one. Two rules where one would do, so the window's behaviour differs between two scopes that look alike in its page and has to be explained and tested twice; the project path still carries the two-command cost and the unobserved same-name-at-two-scopes interplay of registering per scope, and a local install still leaves a user-level registration the person did not ask for.

The window asks, for each project or local install, at which scope the marketplace is registered, offering user scope or the install's own scope as a dropdown choice beside the install, and then runs either `claude plugin install gurita --marketplace uHappyLogic/gurita-claude --scope <s>` or `claude plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/gurita-claude --scope <s>` followed by `claude plugin install gurita@gurita --scope <s>` accordingly. The person who knows whether the project is shared, and whether they want Gurita known machine-wide, makes the call, so neither the teammate-facing gap nor the unwanted user-level registration is imposed on anyone. Every Install and Update, on every harness and at every scope, uses a two-step control inside the Settings page itself: the first click turns the button into a confirming state that states what will change (harness, scope, and for Claude Code project scope the `.claude/settings.json` file), with a way to cancel, and only a second click starts the run; no VS Code dialog is opened. Combines the costs of the two narrower choices: new per-harness pending state on the page and two behaviours for one control, while the in-page second click still guards less firmly than a modal dialog and local-scope and per-user replacing updates go unguarded.

open-question.question: Antigravity has no update command. The installed copy ends up exactly the published release, and a failed fetch or a bad archive leaves the old copy untouched and working, the window between removing the old directory and renaming the new one in being a single rename. It is the most code of the replacing options short of a backup, needing a staging location that Antigravity's plugin discovery never sees and a check of the staged tree, and it still deletes anything a person placed in the directory and depends, like every removing option, on what the existing directory is, which the sibling question on a copy from another source owns.

The update brings the new release into the existing `~/.gemini/config/plugins/gurita` by extracting it straight over the directory as it stands, exactly as the documented `curl` and `tar --strip-components=1 -C` pipeline does when run a second time; nothing is removed first, so every file the old release shipped and the new one no longer does, and anything else the directory holds, stays; no staging copy and no backup are made. It needs no file-removal step of the extension's own, matches the documented install byte for byte, and can never delete anything, so it cannot destroy a hand-placed file or reach through a directory that is not what the window expects. A release that drops or renames a skill, agent, shared procedure, or tool leaves the old file loaded beside the new ones, so the harness can keep offering a skill the release retired, and a fetch that breaks mid-stream leaves a mixture of old and new files with no sign of it.

The update first fetches and extracts the whole new release into a fresh temporary directory outside `~/.gemini/config/plugins/`, checks it (its root `plugin.json` present and its version read), and only then copies its files over the existing plugin directory; nothing in the existing directory is removed, so files the new release no longer ships stay; no backup is kept and the staging directory is discarded. The update removes the existing content of `~/.gemini/config/plugins/gurita` and then extracts the new release into the emptied directory, in place, with no staging copy and no backup; afterwards the directory holds exactly what the new release ships. The installed copy matches the published release exactly, with no retired file left loaded, by the smallest change to the documented pipeline, one removal ahead of it. Between the removal and a completed extraction the plugin is absent or partial, so a network failure or a timeout mid-fetch leaves Antigravity with a broken or empty plugin until a retry succeeds; it also deletes anything a person placed in the directory, and how safe the removal is depends on what the existing directory is, which the sibling question on a copy from another source owns (a directory linked or copied from a checkout).

As the staged swap, the new release is fetched, extracted, and checked in a staging directory outside `~/.gemini/config/plugins/` and then moved into place, but the old `gurita` directory is moved aside to one fixed backup location outside the plugins directory (for example under the per-user `~/.gurita/`) instead of being deleted, each update replacing the previous backup. The extension then owns a stored copy of the plugin outside the harness that nothing in the window restores or removes, since the goal adds no uninstall control, and that the person must learn of and manage; the backup must stand outside the plugins directory or Antigravity would load it as a second plugin.

The update extracts the new release over the existing directory and then removes only the files the installed release shipped and the new one does not, the installed release's file list read from that version's published archive in the distribution repository; any file shipped by neither release stays. Retired files leave while a file a person placed in the directory is kept, the one option that removes stale release content without deleting anything that is not release content. It needs a second fetch of the installed version's archive, which exists only for released versions (the distribution repositories hold the one tag `2.0.0`, while this machine's copy is 1.9.0 from a checkout), so it needs a fallback to another option whenever that archive is missing, and it keeps the overlay's mixed tree on a fetch that breaks mid-stream.

The update removes the existing copy through Antigravity's own `agy plugin uninstall` and then installs the new release by the same path a fresh install from the window uses, so the old directory's content is cleared by the harness rather than by the extension and the result holds exactly what the new release ships. The harness itself clears whatever it registered for the plugin, so the extension deletes no files of its own and the update is an uninstall plus the already-built install. What `agy plugin uninstall` removes, whether it keeps the plugin's enabled or disabled state, and whether it touches a copy it did not install are unobserved, and between the two commands the plugin is gone, a failed install leaving no copy at all; it is viable only as far as the install path the sibling question on Antigravity's install mechanism settles can reinstall into that directory.

open-question.question: The harness check's result is kept for the extension's session and only Check again runs it afresh. After an install or update ends, does the Settings window run the check again by itself, or keep showing the earlier result until Check again is used?
open-question.recommendation: The line of the harness just acted on must not go on saying what was true before, and a failed run can change a harness too; running the unchanged check as Check again does shows the real state at once through the one code path that already exists.
open-question.alternative: An automatic re-check of all three harnesses: whenever an install or update ends, whether it succeeded or failed, the window runs the whole harness check afresh as Check again does, `harness_check.py` unchanged, and the new result replaces the kept one for every harness. The line for the harness acted on shows its real state at once, a failed run that left a marketplace added or a partial copy behind included, with no change to the check script and the same one code path Check again already uses. Every install or update is followed by a full check of all three harnesses in an interactive session shell, up to 120 seconds, and the existing guard that skips a check while one is running would drop the re-check when a check is already in flight unless it is queued; it also depends on the window learning that the run ended, which turns on how the install runs (the sibling Install run form question).

No automatic re-check and no change to the kept result: after an install or update ends, the Settings window goes on showing the harness check's earlier result for every harness, exactly as it does today, until the person uses Check again. Leaves the session-kept check and the Check again control exactly as the previous mission built them, adding no new trigger, no change to `checkHarnesses` or `harness_check.py`, and no extra run of the 120-second, interactive-shell check that the person did not ask for. The harness line the person just acted on keeps saying what was true before, for example "plugin not installed" or a differing version right after a successful install, so the window contradicts what just happened and the person must know to press Check again to see the outcome.

No automatic re-check, but the kept result is flagged: once an install or update ends, the line of the harness it acted on is marked in the window as possibly out of date since that install or update, pointing at Check again, and the flag clears when the next check's result arrives; the other harnesses' lines stand unchanged. The window never presents a pre-install result as current, while the check still runs only when the person asks for it, so no shell session or harness CLI listing is started that they did not request. Adds a third per-harness state to the kept check and the page's drawing, and still leaves the person one click away from the outcome they almost always want to see right after acting.

An automatic re-check of all three harnesses only when the install or update ended successfully, `harness_check.py` unchanged; when it failed, the earlier result is kept as it stands until Check again is used. Shows the new installed version right after the case that changes it, while a failed run, whose failure the window reports on its own, costs no extra check. A failed run can still have changed the harness, for example a marketplace registered before the install step failed, and the kept line then hides that; telling success from failure requires the window to receive the run's exit status, which depends on how the install runs (the sibling Install run form question).

An automatic re-check of only the harness the install or update acted on: whenever one ends, the window checks that one harness afresh, which needs `harness_check.py` to accept a harness to check rather than always listing all three, and replaces that harness's line in the kept result while the other two harnesses' lines are kept as they were. The line the person acted on is refreshed at once while the run stays short, starting one CLI listing instead of three and leaving the other harnesses' results undisturbed. Changes the check script's interface and its tests and turns the kept result into per-harness pieces taken at different times, so the window's lines may no longer come from one check; it also depends on the window learning that the run ended (the sibling Install run form question).
